title: Double descent
objectives: Explain why test error peaks where parameters equal data points and falls again past it.

screens.title: Past the threshold
screens.prose: This lesson takes about fifteen minutes; interview pace is four minutes a question. You met the U-shaped picture in `research-int` l6 and the experiment in `nn-train` l12. Here: 40 noisy points in 10 dimensions, least squares on $p$ random ReLU features, median test error over 20 seeds.

It keeps rising: more features, more overfitting.
options.why: That is the U-shaped picture, which stops at the threshold. Past it the error falls again.

options.text: It stays near the peak, since the fit still passes through every point.
options.why: Every fit past 40 interpolates, but the one chosen is smoother as $p$ grows.

options.text: It returns to the first minimum and no lower.
options.why: It goes lower: about a quarter of the first minimum by 400 features.

Past 40 there are many exact fits; least squares picks the one of smallest norm.
The smallest-norm fit gets smoother as $p$ grows, and the error falls again.

feedback.correct: It falls again, to $0.0644$ at 400 features: below $0.249$ at 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about which of the many exact fits least squares returns past 40.

byKey.rises: That is the classical picture. It holds only below the threshold here.

explain.text: This is double descent: a first U, a peak of $7.63$ where $p = n = 40$, then a second fall. By 400 features the error is $0.0644$, by 2,000 it is $0.0646$.

screens.title: Why the peak sits at p = n
screens.prose: At $p = n$ the system has exactly one solution, and it must pass through every noisy point. Slide through $p$ and watch the median norm $\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|$ of the fitted coefficients.
screens.question: How many times larger is the median norm at $p = 40$ than at $p = 10$? Give 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Read the norm at 10 and at 40 features.
They are $1.166$ and $10.14$.

feedback.correct: About $8.7$ times: the forced fit needs huge coefficients.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the norm at 40 by the norm at 10.

byKey.inverse: You divided the other way round. The norm at 40 is the larger.

explain.text: To pass through every noisy point the coefficients blow up, to $10.14$, about $8.7$ times the norm at 10. Past 40 many fits interpolate, and the smallest one shrinks: $0.341$ at 400 features. Large coefficients amplify noise at new points, which is the peak in test error.

screens.prose: The first minimum is $0.249$ at 10 features. Past the peak the error falls to $0.0644$ at 400.

explain.text: The second descent goes well below the first minimum, to about $0.26$ of it. Gradient descent started at zero on this fit also ends at the smallest-norm solution, with no explicit penalty. Say that number: it is what makes double descent more than a curiosity.

screens.prose: Rerun the experiment with label noise of sd 0.2 instead of 0.1.

Only the peak moves: it shifts right, to more features.
options.why: The peak stays at $p = n = 40$; noise changes heights, not where the threshold is.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read both curves at 40 and at 2,000 features.

screens.title: More parameters always overfit?
screens.prose: A candidate says: "More parameters always overfit. That is the bias-variance trade-off."

params.xLabel: log₁₀ of features p (40 training points)

screens.question: What do you say?

options.text: The decomposition still holds, but variance peaks at $p = n$ and falls past it.
Agree: that is the U-shaped curve, which holds for every model size.
options.why: The U is the left half of this chart. The error falls again past $p = n$.

options.text: Disagree: more parameters never hurt test error, at any size.
options.why: They hurt near $p = n$: the peak is about 31 times the first minimum.

options.text: Agree, unless you add more data to keep up with the parameters.
options.why: More data moves the threshold, but at fixed data the error still falls again past it.

hints.text: Look at the right half of the chart.
The error falls past 40 features.
The trade-off still holds; what fails is variance rising with the parameter count.

feedback.correct: The U-curve is only half the picture for minimum-norm fits.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the error past 40 features.

byKey.agree: You stopped at the U. Past $p = n$ the variance and the error fall again.

explain.text: More parameters hurt most at $p = n$, where the error is $7.63$, though the decomposition still holds. Variance peaks there and falls past it, since parameter count is a poor measure of capacity for a smallest-norm fit. The error falls to $0.0644$ by 400 features.

screens.question: What happens to the peak?

options.text: It almost disappears: $0.105$ at 40 features against $7.63$.
It stays: the peak is a property of $p = n$, not of the fit.
options.why: The peak comes from huge coefficients, which a penalty caps.

The ridge curve barely bumps there.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the ridge curve at 40 features.

explain.text: With the penalty tuned at each $p$ the error at 40 is $0.105$, a small bump. The curve keeps falling, to $0.0463$ at 400. Double descent is sharpest with no regularisation.

screens.title: Model-wise and epoch-wise
screens.prose: Belkin et al. (2019) named the second descent. Nakkiran et al. (2019) found it in deep networks, as width grows (model-wise) and as training goes on (epoch-wise). The spoken rule: test error peaks where the model can just interpolate the training set. That is $p = n$ here, and for a deep net it is where its effective complexity is about $n$.
screens.question: Which is epoch-wise double descent?

options.text: Test error rises then falls again as one network trains for longer.
Test error rises then falls as the network gets wider.
options.why: That is model-wise double descent, the version on this chart.

options.text: Test error falls steadily with more training data.
options.why: That is the usual learning curve. Near the threshold, Nakkiran et al. find more data can even hurt.

feedback.correct: Epoch-wise: the same peak, met over training time.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Epoch-wise means over training steps.

explain.text: Training longer lets a large network fit more of the noise, so its effective size grows with epochs. The peak then appears in time instead of in width.

screens.title: Forty days, two thousand features
screens.prose: A colleague reads the chart. She proposes a 2,000-feature minimum-norm regression on the last 40 days of returns, "since past the peak more features help".
screens.question: What is the strongest objection?

options.text: It needs a learnable signal; daily returns have out-of-sample $R^2$ under 1 per cent.
At 2,000 features the fit sits right on the error peak at $p = n$.
options.why: The peak is at $p = n = 40$; 2,000 is far past it.

options.text: A 2,000-feature fit is far too slow to run on each new day.
options.why: A 40-by-2,000 pseudo-inverse is fast. Speed is not the problem.

options.text: No objection: the chart shows that more features help.
options.why: The chart's target is a smooth function with small noise. Returns are mostly noise.

hints.text: What made the second descent work in our experiment?
A smooth target, $\tanh(\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{w})$, with noise sd 0.1.
Returns are nearly all noise, and 40 days is one regime.

feedback.correct: Double descent explains why big models can generalise, not that any big model will.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the signal in the chart with the signal in returns.

byKey.fine: The experiment had a strong smooth signal. Daily returns do not.

explain.text: Huge networks generalise when there is structure to find and the implicit bias suits it. With under 1 per cent of signal and 40 days of one regime, the minimum-norm fit interpolates noise.

screens.title: The curve in code
screens.prose: Write `min_norm_test_error(p, seed)`. The supplied `make_data(seed)` is the generator behind every chart in this lesson. Use the first $p$ columns of `W` for ReLU features, the minimum-norm least-squares fit, and the test set.
screens.question: Complete the function.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np


def min_norm_test_error(p, seed):
    X, y, Xt, yt, W = make_data(seed)   # supplied: 40 train, 2,000 test, W is 10 by 2,000
    # features: ReLU of X @ (first p columns of W); fit the minimum-norm least squares
    # return the mean squared error on the test set
    ...
widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def min_norm_test_error(p, seed):
    X, y, Xt, yt, W = make_data(seed)
    F = np.maximum(X @ W[:, :p], 0)
    Ft = np.maximum(Xt @ W[:, :p], 0)
    beta = np.linalg.pinv(F) @ y
    return float(np.mean((Ft @ beta - yt) ** 2))
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
import math


def make_data(seed, n=40, n_test=2000, d=10, noise=0.1, P=2000):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = rng.normal(size=d) / math.sqrt(d)
    X = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
    Xt = rng.normal(size=(n_test, d))
    y = np.tanh(X @ w) + noise * rng.normal(size=n)
    yt = np.tanh(Xt @ w)
    W = rng.normal(size=(d, P)) / math.sqrt(d)
    return X, y, Xt, yt, W

tests.call: float(np.median([min_norm_test_error(10, s) for s in range(20)]))
float(np.median([min_norm_test_error(40, s) for s in range(20)]))
float(np.median([min_norm_test_error(400, s) for s in range(20)]))

mutants.source:
import numpy as np


def min_norm_test_error(p, seed):
    X, y, Xt, yt, W = make_data(seed)
    F = np.maximum(X @ W[:, :p], 0)
    Ft = np.maximum(Xt @ W[:, :p], 0)
    beta = np.linalg.solve(F.T @ F, F.T @ y)
    return float(np.mean((Ft @ beta - yt) ** 2))
mutants.symptom: Solves the normal equations, which are singular past p = n.

hints.text: Features are `np.maximum(X @ W[:, :p], 0)`, the same for the test inputs.
The pseudo-inverse gives the minimum-norm solution for any $p$.
`beta = np.linalg.pinv(F) @ y`, then the mean squared error on `Xt`, `yt`.

byKey.test-1: One seed at 10 features is off. Use ReLU features from the first $p$ columns of the supplied `W`. Score on the test set, not the training set.
byKey.test-2: The fit breaks at 400 features. Past $p = n$ the normal equations are singular; `np.linalg.pinv` gives the minimum-norm solution.

explain.text: The pseudo-inverse works on both sides of the threshold: it is the least-squares fit below 40 and the smallest exact fit above. That one line is the whole of double descent here.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer goes on: "Where would ridge put the peak?" The new curve uses one fixed penalty, $\lambda = 0.01$.

params.xLabel: log₁₀ of features p (40 training points)

screens.question: What do you answer?

options.text: Still at $p = n$, but far lower: $0.471$ instead of $7.63$.
It moves to $p = 2n$, since ridge acts like extra data.
options.why: The chart's ridge curve still peaks at 40 features.

options.text: Nowhere: any penalty, however small, removes the peak.
options.why: A penalty of $0.001$ still leaves a peak of about 1.64 at 40.

hints.text: Find the top of the ridge curve.
It is still at 40 features.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find where the ridge curve peaks.

byKey.moves: The ridge curve peaks at 40 too; only its height changed.

explain.text: The penalty caps the coefficients at $p = n$, so the peak shrinks to $0.471$ but stays at 40. The stronger the penalty, the flatter the bump.

ideas: Test error peaks at the interpolation threshold, $p = n$: $7.63$ at 40 features for 40 points, against $0.249$ at 10.
Past it the minimum-norm fit gets smoother and the error falls again, to $0.0644$ at 400 features.
A tuned ridge penalty leaves only a bump; double descent does not license huge regressions on noisy returns.

options.text: The one exact fit needs huge coefficients, which amplify noise.
There are too few features to fit the signal at all.
options.why: At $p = n$ there are enough to fit every training point exactly.

options.why: Least squares here is solved exactly, with no iterations.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about the size of the one exact solution.

quiz.prose: At 2,000 features the median test error is $0.0646$ with noise sd 0.1 and $0.122$ with sd 0.2.
quiz.question: What is the second figure as a multiple of the first? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the two errors.

byKey.var: The noise part does quadruple. The floor also holds an approximation error of about $0.046$ that noise does not touch, so the total roughly doubles.

explain.text: The floor goes from $0.0646$ to $0.122$, about $1.9$ times. With no noise the floor is $0.0461$, so the noise part goes from $0.0185$ to $0.0763$, four times. The interpolating fit carries that noise into its predictions.
